newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business - Jan 19.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business - Jan 19.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
SUNDAY TELEGRAPH
-- SFO PROBES COPPERFINGER LOSS

The Serious Fraud Office is to investigate the fund management debacle in which Charlie "Copperfinger" Vincent lost up to half of his fortune. The Securities & Investments Board is also seeking to interview Alexander Jones, fund manager and director of Bede & Co, with the view to seeing documentation on the deals which went wrong.
-- JONES OF NEXT TURNS DOWN SEARS

The chief executive of Next, David Jones, has turned down the job of chief executive of Sears. Two other blue-chip chief executives have followed his example. Institutional investors have said that they are not planning a coup and dismissed suggestions they had appointed headhunters.
-- SALOMON LINKS WITH FIDELITY

Wall Street investment firm, Salomon Brothers, has signed an alliance with Fidelity Investments, one of the world's largest fund managers. This gives Salomon access to Fidelity's 6.1 million private clients. The deal is one of the most innovative and far-reaching to be forged on Wall Street in recent years, and could enable Salomon to emerge as a new equities powerhouse to compete with Merrill Lynch.
-- CORPORATE PROFITS ARE 'BACK TO FULL HEALTH'

According to a corporate health check of Britain's largest companies from CCN Group, Europe's largest credit reference agency, company profits have recovered from the recession, three years after it ended. CCN claim that the real return on capital employed by British industry was 10 per cent in the third quarter, compared with 7.1 per cent in 1991.
-- HOLLICK REJECTS 42 MILLION STG O'REILLY BID

The Chief executive of United News and Media, Lord Hollick, has rejected an offer of 42 million stg for his South Eastern regional newspapers from Tony O'Reilly, the Irish media magnate, and has opted to keep the 30 titles instead. Hollick is now looking at merging the publications with his advertising periodicals division UAP.
SUNDAY TIMES
-- MORGAN BOSSES WERE OUT TO GET ME, SAYS HORLICK

Nicola Horlick, the former fund manager at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM), has claimed a personality clash led to her departure. She claims that Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's chief executive, Michael Dobson, and MGAM's chief executive, Robert Smith, were out to get rif of her and were looking for an excuse. She says she was left in a vulnerable position after the departure of MGAM's former chief executive Keith Parcy, after the scandal over Peter Young.
-- FORD SEEKS AID TO SAVE HALEWOOD

Ford is to ask the Government for 75 million stg in aid to help finance a new vehicle project that could keep the Halewood factory open after Escort production ends in three years. The plant will certainly close without the money, with the loss of 2,500 jobs. Two Department of trade and Industry officials are evaluating the project and a decision will be made in a few weeks.
-- BLAIR BOWS TO BUSINESS OVER HOSTILE BIDS

Labour Party leader Tony Blair is set to bring the party's competition policy more into line with the views of business. Blair has persuaded a number of top businessmen to appear on Labour platforms in the next few months to avoid any rift between Labour and business which proved damaging in the run up to the last election.
-- FRANCO-GERMAN EMU ROW BOOSTS POUND

Sterling will benefit from tension over European monetary union and strengthen further despite the decision by Chancellor Kenneth Clarke not to raise interest rates. Bundesbank officials have been expressing dismay over reports that France is to insist on a French president for the European central bank, as a trade-off for having the institution based in Frankfurt.
-- SIEMENS' GRAND DESIGN TO SEAL ROLLS POWER DEAL

German industrial giant Siemens AG is considering the purchase of Rolls-Royce's Parsons turbine subsidiary as part of a wide-ranging deal which could involve the acquisition of other Rolls industrial power operations. According to industry insiders, Siemens could take control of Rolls's switchgear company, Reyrolle, and its transformer manufacturer Peebles. Siemens faces competition from General Electric, which also hopes to buy Parsons.
THE OBSERVER
-- BRUSSELS WILL TRY TO BLOCK BA DEAL WITH QUICK-FIRE INJUNCTION

The European Commission is set to seek an injunction in the European Court to block the proposed alliance between British Airways and American Airlines if the UK government tries to wave the deal through. EU competition commissioner Karel van Miert has said that if the UK approved the deal without going to the MMC he would take the Government to the European Court of Justice. He is considering asking BA, American and other parties to meet him in Brussels next month to put their cases.
-- DOWN ON ITS LUCK CAPITAL IN TAKEOVER TALKS AS YANKS ROLL FOR LONDON CASINOS

Casino company Capital Corp is in talks with an American group outside the gambling industry about a possible takeover. Shares in the company have climbed by 20 per cent due to speculation about a bid. City sources believe chairman Garry Nesbitt would be prepared to agree a takeover for little more than Capital's current value of 184 million stg.
-- BOOKIES 'SHORTEN ODDS ON OUTSIDERS' FOR FEAR OF INSIDERS

According to research from Leighton Vaughan Williams and David Paton of Nottingham Trent University, Bookies will artificially reduce the odds on outsiders in horse races to cushion them against big losses from insider betting. A result would be a loss of 600 million stg a year for ordinary punters. They found that the profit margin implied in odds tended to be greater in races with more runners and more unknown horses and these are the races where bookies most fear insider activity.
-- BUSINESS FORUM PUTS GROWTH BEFORE INFLATION

The Commission on Public Policy and British Business is to call on a new government to abandon the narrow targeting of inflation in favour of a monetary policy goal which takes account of economic growth as well as prices. It will also recommend that Britain should opt in to the social chapter, which will involve no extra costs to business at present, and to take part in economic and monetary union.
-- FACTORIES FALL QUIET AS STRONG POUND HURTS EXPORTS

Key business surveys from the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) and the Confederation of British Industry show that the strong pound is hurting manufacturing. The BCC survey shows that there was a slowdown in factory orders and sales in the final three months of last year. The survey will be in line with the Bank of England's argument that the appreciation of the pound should not be used as an excuse to delay action to combat rising price pressures in the domestic economy.
INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY
-- SFO RAIDS HINCHLIFFE BANKERS

The Serious Fraud office has raided the premises of bankers and associates of Stephen Hinchliffe, the Sheffield businessman, as part of a new investigation arising out of the collapse of the Facia group last year. The inquiry is into widespread corruption involving former staff at United Mizrahi Bank, Israel's fourth-biggest and Facia's main backer.
-- FEARS OVER PSION CHIEF

There is growing speculation within the City that David Potter, founder of Psion Plc, the world's leading maker of hand-held computers, has given up his executive responsibilities. He is recuperating after heart bypass surgery. A Psion spokesman said no date had been set for his return and declined to comment that Potter may take a non-executive role.
-- DOCKLANDS CASINO PLANNED

Jemstock, an associate company of Capital & Provident Management, has been granted planning permission for the first legally run casino in east London. The London Docklands Development Corporation granted planning consent for a casino to be build at South Quay Tower, which was severely damaged by last February's IRA bombing in Docklands.
-- DYNAMIC DUO REUNITED

John Coyle and Brian Basham, two of the top corporate spin doctor of the 1980s, are to rejoin forces in a bid to recreate their success. They are set to launch Basham & Coyle Partnership Plc on Monday and they have already received a warm response from City merchant banks.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- US BOSSES AIM TO SINK WINDFALL TAX

Bosses of American-owned electricity companies in Britain are preparing a political offensive to block Labour's plans for a windfall tax on the utilities. They have met to discuss action that could involve threats of trade sanctions against British companies investing in the U.S.
-- HUGE CRACKDOWN ON LLOYD'S CHEATS

David Gittings, director of Lloyd's of London's regulatory division, is leading a crackdown on fraud, malpractice and incompetence. He will be investigating many of Lloyd's 210 insurance brokers and underwriting agents, who look after the affairs of Names. Information collected has been passed on to the police for possible action against the firms and individuals involved.
-- LABOUR STIRS UP 44 MILLION STG PENSIONS SURPLUS ROW

The Labour Party and the pensions ombudsman, Julian Farrand, have joined forces in the battle over the National Grid hiving off 44 million stg pension fund surplus to pay for early redundancies. Other privatised power companies may be forced to repay one billion stg to pension funds, boosting benefits for more than 200,000 scheme members.
-- LAKER AND VIRGIN JOIN TO ATTACK MERGER

Sir Freddie Laker and Richard Branson's Virgin Atlantic have teamed up to launch an advertising campaign to sink the proposed merger between British Airways and American Airlines. Sir Freddie also sent a letter to the Prime Minister urging him to refer the deal to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
-- OUTLAWED TITAN TO FIGHT BAN

Outlawed pyramid selling operation Titan is preparing a court battle against a new law banning similar operations in the UK. Directors believe the ban will be swept aside by European rules and they warn that the Government will have to spend millions of pounds to defend the action.
